summary: CosmoCode - Earth Analog Finder is an interactive web application that ranks 24 real Earth sites against Moon base and Mars base conditions across 13 physical parameters. It helps mission planners, researchers, and engineers select terrestrial field-testing and crew-training sites using transparent, auditable data rather than reputation. Users can compare sites with built-in lunar and Martian profiles or adjust parameter weights live to recompute 0-100 similarity scores, inspect separate data-confidence ratings, and identify planetary conditions that no Earth site can physically replicate.
details: CosmoCode – Earth Analog Finder is an open, reproducible web application built by Team CosmoCode, second-year CSE students in Dhaka, for NASA Space Apps 2026 to solve a core challenge in planetary mission planning: no Earth site matches every lunar or Martian condition, yet terrestrial analog sites for testing equipment, rehearsing missions, and training crews are often chosen on reputation rather than a checkable method. The app ranks 24 real Earth sites across 13 physical parameters using a transparent 0–100 weighted similarity score (normalized distance to target divided by tolerance, clamped between 0 and 1) paired with a separate data-confidence rating, offering built-in Moon base and Mars base profiles, a live custom weight builder, an impossible-axes panel that sets aside parameters Earth cannot physically match (19% weight for the Moon across temperature range, radiation, and 336-hour daylight; 17% for Mars across radiation and pressure), a score-colored world map with free tiles, filtering, sorting, CSV export, and seven project documents served at /docs/. Four zero-API-key scripts in scripts/ compile 9 measured parameters (NASA POWER climatology and AOD_55 dust, SRTM/ASTER 30 m elevation and slope, GeoNames isolation, ISRIC SoilGrids sand percentage), 3 calculated parameters (slope, daylight, and cosmic-ray radiation dose modeled via Störmer dipole cutoff rigidity and the Lindborg et al. 2004 altitude fit), and 1 expert-estimated parameter (aqueous geochemistry), while fixing a NASA POWER coarse-grid elevation artifact that placed Mauna Kea at 636 m (+20.9°C) instead of 4,147 m (-1.92°C) alongside five other mountain and basin sites. Our headline finding is that no Earth site scores above 60/100—led by East Antarctic Plateau (58.1), McMurdo Dry Valleys (56.7), and Atacama Desert (48.2) for the Moon, and East Antarctic Plateau (55.9), Atacama Desert (50.7), and McMurdo Dry Valleys (46.3) for Mars—proving quantitatively where laboratory simulation is essential, with 5,000 Monte Carlo perturbations (±25% weight variance) holding the #1 rank 81.1% of the time for the Moon and 98.8% for Mars. Next, we plan to replace our one-shot retrieval scripts with an automated live pipeline, add uncertainty ranges to every score, expand beyond global-mean targets to mission-specific zones like a lunar south-pole base, refine grid-smoothed precipitation, and incorporate measured datasets for aqueous geochemistry and the three Antarctic soil values, building on our Next.js, TypeScript, Leaflet, and Recharts implementation.
